briefing.text: cSCC has a very high UV-driven mutational burden (about 30-235 mutations/Mb in this cohort), so many long genes such as TTN and MUC16 are mutated in a large share of tumours by chance. Raw mutation frequency alone does not show that a gene is a recurrent driver. Compare TP53 and CDKN2A with length-matched passenger genes, or use a dN/dS- or MutSigCV-style background-adjusted comparison, and look at the mutation pattern: the truncating fraction, TP53 DNA-binding-domain hotspots, and known CDKN2A inactivating changes such as R80*, H83Y and D84N. A high frequency of truncating or hotspot mutations in a known tumour suppressor is strong evidence of a recurrent driver. (Background knowledge, not web-verified.)
briefing.reason: Without a background comparison, high frequencies in a hypermutated tumour type can be misread. The mutation pattern tells driver from passenger.

briefing.text: Tabulate Variant_Classification for TP53 and CDKN2A. Count protein-altering classes (missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice site, in-frame indel) separately from silent and non-coding classes before counting mutated samples.
briefing.reason: Including silent or UTR calls would inflate the counts. The classification also feeds the truncating-fraction check.

briefing.text: CDKN2A is often inactivated by homozygous deletion or promoter methylation. Neither event appears in data_mutations.txt, and this dataset has no copy-number file, so the CDKN2A point-mutation frequency is only a lower bound on CDKN2A alteration. A modest but clearly nonzero CDKN2A mutation rate (published cSCC series report roughly 20-50% for CDKN2A and 50-90% for TP53) still supports recurrence. A CDKN2A rate below the TP53 rate is not evidence against the claim. (Background knowledge, not web-verified.)
briefing.reason: This stops a team from rejecting the claim because CDKN2A point mutations are less frequent than expected, or less frequent than TP53.

briefing.text: In cancer-genomics papers, 'recurrently mutated' is used loosely. It usually means mutated in several tumours (two or more, often a notable fraction). 'Significantly mutated' is the stricter term for genes above the background rate (MutSigCV/dNdScv). Many cSCC papers call TP53 and CDKN2A recurrently mutated on the basis of frequency plus known driver status. Medium confidence, from background knowledge, not web-verified.
briefing.reason: This defines the bar the hypothesis has to meet, so the team does not hold 'recurrent' to the stricter 'significantly mutated' standard.

shared_assumptions: Both teams take 'recurrently mutated' to mean a high share of samples with nonsilent mutations plus a simple background comparison. Neither tested whether a formal significance criterion such as dN/dS, which the source study may have used, would also flag both genes.

Both teams counted CDKN2A mutations at the gene level without checking which transcript the annotation used. The gene encodes p16INK4a and p14ARF from overlapping exons, so the protein-change annotation depends on the isoform, and some variants may fall in non-coding parts of an alternative transcript.

Both teams treat the 25 metastasis samples as independent tumours. Team A saw identical TP53 variants shared between sample pairs but did not settle whether these were contamination, duplicates or real recurrent hotspots.
unused_evidence: The clinical columns (immunosuppressive treatment, primary site, nodal stage, grade) were not used. They do not bear on whether the two genes are recurrently mutated, so leaving them out is unlikely to change the label.

TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS in the sample table was not checked against the MAF counts. This only matters if the MAF holds far more rows than the study's filtered calls, which would mean unfiltered or low-confidence calls are present.
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams named the lack of a formal dN/dS model and only reported it. Their simple ns:syn and truncating-fraction checks already put both genes far above the background, so this is unlikely to change the label.
Team A noted that n_alt_count is missing, which leaves germline and artefact status uncertain. The matched somatic status reduces this concern.
second_readings: 'Recurrently mutated' could mean statistically significantly mutated rather than frequently mutated. At 96% and 80%, with zero synonymous mutations and a strong truncating excess, both readings point the same way.
'Metastatic CSCC' matches the cohort exactly (every sample is a metastasis), so there is no in-scope or out-of-scope ambiguity that would support Not verifiable.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed True label highly. The cohort is exactly metastatic cSCC, both genes are mutated in most samples with no synonymous mutations and a strong truncating excess, and none of the open points could plausibly reverse a recurrence claim.

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: For the sample pairs that share identical TP53 variants (H179Y, Q38*), do they also share an unusually large number of other identical variants across the whole MAF? If so, would removing one sample of each pair change your frequency estimates?

When a cancer-genomics study reports genes as 'recurrently' or 'significantly' mutated, which criteria are typical (frequency threshold, dN/dS q-value, MutSigCV)? Can a gene mutated in a large share of tumours fail the formal test in a small, highly hypermutated cohort?
questions.why: Neither team ran a formal selection test. Knowing whether frequency-based and significance-based definitions can disagree tells us whether the missing test matters.

findings.question: When a cancer-genomics study reports genes as 'recurrently' or 'significantly' mutated, which criteria are typical (frequency threshold, dN/dS q-value, MutSigCV)? Can a gene mutated in a large share of tumours fail the formal test in a small, highly hypermutated cohort?
findings.answer: NOT WEB-VERIFIED: the research gateway returned HTTP 502/403 on all 3 calls, so no page was read. From background knowledge: 'recurrently mutated' usually means a frequency criterion (mutated in several tumours or a notable fraction, often with known driver status), while 'significantly mutated' means a background-adjusted test, typically dNdScv q<0.1 or MutSigCV q<=0.1. Yes, the two can disagree. In a small, very high-TMB UV cohort the background rate is high and power is low, so a frequently mutated gene can fail the formal test. Long passenger genes (TTN, MUC16) can also be frequent without being significant. TP53 usually remains significant even in small cSCC cohorts; CDKN2A may not. A missing formal test therefore does not undermine a frequency-based 'recurrently mutated' claim for known tumour suppressors that show truncating or hotspot patterns.
